b: Pathogenesis (response-to-injury):
Chronic endothelial injury (HTN, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, hyperglycaemia, turbulent flow at branch points)
Injured endothelium → permeable to LDL → LDL enters intima, oxidizes
Oxidized LDL attracts monocytes → become macrophages → engulf lipid → foam cells
Foam cell accumulation = fatty streak (earliest lesion)

These notes cover all 10 major cardiovascular pathology topics at MBChB level.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Cardiovascular pathology studies how injury to vessels and the heart leads to disease, using clinical clues and tests to guide diagnosis, staging, and treatment.

sections.p: Cardiovascular pathology refers to structural and functional changes in the heart and vessels caused by chronic injury, inflammation, or infection.
b: Key diagnosis relies on history, physical exam, imaging, and biomarkers.

t.b: What signs support vascular disease? Detects murmurs, pulses, edema indicating obstruction or heart failure.
What does it assess? Evaluates chamber size, wall motion, valve function; abnormal findings confirm structural disease.

sections.p: Severity is staged by widely used systems: NYHA for heart failure, ACC/AHA for coronary disease, and WHO for hypertension.
b: Stage guides urgency of therapy and prognosis.

t.b: How does it grade heart failure? Ranges I‑IV based on symptom limitation; higher class predicts worse outcomes.
What does it indicate? From asymptomatic atherosclerosis (Stage A) to refractory angina (Stage D).

sections.p: Most cardiovascular injury begins with endothelial dysfunction from modifiable risk factors, then progresses to atherosclerosis, hypertension, or infection.
b: Hypertension – most common cause of left‑ventricular hypertrophy.
Atherosclerosis – driven by smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia.
Rheumatic heart disease – prevalent in low‑resource settings.
HIV‑associated vasculitis, TB pericarditis, malaria‑related cardiomyopathy.

sections.p: Patients may have chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, or peripheral claudication, but early disease can be silent.
b: Chest pressure radiating to arm suggests coronary ischemia.
Leg swelling with jugular venous distension points to heart failure.
Fever and pericardial rub suggest infectious pericarditis.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; when unavailable, use bedside tools or refer.

t.b: Does myocardial injury exist? Elevated levels confirm infarction; normal does not exclude unstable angina.
Is atherosclerotic risk high? LDL >130 mg/dL indicates need for statin therapy.
What structural changes are present? Shows cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion; may be normal early.
What electrical abnormalities exist? ST changes suggest ischemia; arrhythmias indicate conduction disease.

sections.p: Identify features that signal imminent danger and require urgent care.
b: Sudden chest pain with diaphoresis – possible MI.
New-onset severe dyspnoea – acute heart failure or pulmonary edema.
Syncope with murmur – critical aortic stenosis.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide supportive measures and monitor for deterioration.
b: Antihypertensives (ACE‑I, ARB, thiazides) lower afterload and prevent remodeling.
Statins reduce LDL and plaque progression; avoid fibrates unless severe hypertriglyceridaemia.
Antiplatelet agents (aspirin) prevent thrombus; avoid in active bleeding.
Diuretics relieve congestion in heart failure; monitor electrolytes.

sections.p: Regular review of risk factors, imaging, and biomarkers helps prevent progression.
b: Re‑measure blood pressure and lipids every 3–6 months.
Repeat echocardiogram if symptoms change.
Encourage smoking cessation, diet, and exercise.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic cardiovascular disease must be distinguished.
b: Pulmonary embolism – presents with chest pain and dyspnoea but has clear lungs on X‑ray.
Anxiety panic attack – chest tightness without ECG changes.
Musculoskeletal chest wall pain – reproducible on palpation.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal, leading to misdiagnosis.
b: Troponin may be normal in early MI; repeat after 3 h.
LDL can appear low in acute illness; re‑check after recovery.
ECG may be normal in silent ischemia; consider stress testing.

whenToSeekHelp: Loss of consciousness with heart murmur

faq.q: Why does hypertension cause heart failure?
faq.a: High pressure forces the left ventricle to work harder, leading to muscle thickening and eventual pump failure.

faq.q: Can a normal cholesterol level rule out atherosclerosis?
faq.a: No; plaque can develop despite normal lipids, especially with smoking or diabetes.

faq.q: What is the role of inflammation in cardiovascular disease?
faq.a: Inflammation drives endothelial injury, foam‑cell formation, and plaque instability.
